{{Short description|Integration kernels for smoothing out sharp features}}
[[File:Mollified Illustration.svg|thumb|A mollifier (top) in [[Dimension (mathematics)|dimension]] one. At the bottom, in red is a function with a corner (left) and sharp jump (right), and in blue is its mollified version.]]

In [[mathematics]], '''mollifiers''' (also known as ''approximations to the identity'') are particular [[smooth function]]s, used for example in [[Distribution (mathematics)|distribution theory]] to create [[sequence]]s of smooth functions approximating nonsmooth [[Generalized function|(generalized) functions]], via [[convolution]]. Intuitively, given a (generalized) function, convolving it with a mollifier "mollifies" it, that is, its sharp features are smoothed, while still remaining close to the original.<ref>That is, the mollified function is close to the original with respect to the [[topology]] of the given space of generalized functions.</ref> 

They are also known as '''Friedrichs mollifiers''' after [[Kurt Otto Friedrichs]], who introduced them.<ref>See {{Harv|Friedrichs|1944|pp=136–139}}.</ref>

== Historical notes ==

Mollifiers were introduced by [[Kurt Otto Friedrichs]] in his paper {{Harv|Friedrichs|1944|pp=136–139}}, which is considered a watershed in the modern theory of [[partial differential equations]].<ref name="Laxref">See the commentary of [[Peter Lax]] on the paper {{Harv|Friedrichs|1944}} in {{Harv|Friedrichs|1986|loc=volume 1, p. 117}}.</ref> The name of this mathematical object has a curious genesis, and [[Peter Lax]] tells the story in his commentary on that paper published in Friedrichs' "''Selecta''".<ref name="Lax.p.117">{{Harv|Friedrichs|1986|loc=volume 1, p. 117}}</ref> According to him, at that time, the mathematician Donald Alexander Flanders was a colleague of Friedrichs; since he liked to consult colleagues about English usage, he asked Flanders for advice on naming the smoothing operator he was using.<ref name="Laxref" /> Flanders was a modern-day [[puritan]], nicknamed by his friends Moll after [[Moll Flanders]] in recognition of his moral qualities: he suggested calling the new mathematical concept a "'''mollifier'''" as a pun incorporating both Flanders' nickname and the verb '[[Wiktionary:mollify|to mollify]]', meaning 'to smooth over' in a figurative sense.<ref>In {{Harv|Friedrichs|1986|loc=volume 1, p. 117}} Lax writes "''On English usage Friedrichs liked to consult his friend and colleague, Donald Flanders, a descendant of puritans and a puritan himself, with the highest standard of his own conduct, noncensorious towards others. In recognition of his moral qualities he was called Moll by his friends. When asked by Friedrichs what to name the smoothing operator, Flanders remarked that they could be named "mollifier" after himself; Friedrichs was delighted, as on other occasions, to carry this joke into print.''"</ref>

Previously, [[Sergei Sobolev]] had used mollifiers in his epoch making 1938 paper,<ref>See {{Harv|Sobolev|1938}}.</ref> which contains the proof of the [[Sobolev embedding theorem]]: Friedrichs himself acknowledged Sobolev's work on mollifiers, stating "''These mollifiers were introduced by Sobolev and the author...''".<ref>{{Harvtxt|Friedrichs|1953|p=196}}.</ref>

It must be pointed out that the term "mollifier" has undergone [[linguistic drift]] since the time of these foundational works: Friedrichs defined as "'''mollifier'''" the [[integral operator]] whose [[Integral operator|kernel]] is one of the functions nowadays called mollifiers. However, since the properties of a linear integral operator are completely determined by its kernel, the name mollifier was inherited by the kernel itself as a result of common usage.

== Definition ==
[[Image:Heat eqn.gif|right|frame|A function undergoing progressive mollification.]]

=== Modern (distribution based) definition ===
{{EquationRef|1|Definition 1.}} Let <math>\varphi</math> be a [[smooth function]] on <math>\R^n</math>, <math>n \ge 1</math>, and put <math>\varphi_\epsilon(x) := \epsilon^{-n}\varphi(x / \epsilon)</math> for <math>\epsilon > 0 \in\R</math>.
Then <math>\varphi</math> is a '''mollifier''' if it satisfies the following three requirements:

:{{EquationRef|2|(1){{spaces|2}}}} it is [[Support (mathematics)|compactly supported]],<ref>This is satisfied if, for instance, <math>\varphi(x)</math> is a [[bump function]].</ref>   
:{{EquationRef|3|(2){{spaces|2}}}}<math>\int_{\R^n}\!\varphi(x)\mathrm{d}x=1</math>,
:{{EquationRef|4|(3){{spaces|2}}}}<math>\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\varphi_\epsilon(x) = \lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\epsilon^{-n}\varphi(x / \epsilon)=\delta(x)</math>,

where <math>\delta(x)</math> is the [[Dirac delta function]], and the limit must be understood as taking place in the space of Schwartz [[distribution (mathematics)|distribution]]s. The function <math>\varphi</math> may also satisfy further conditions of interest;<ref>See {{harv|Giusti|1984|p=11}}.</ref> for example, if it satisfies

:{{EquationRef|5|(4){{spaces|2}}}}<math>\varphi(x)\ge 0</math> for all <math>x \in \R^n</math>, 

then it is called a '''positive mollifier''', and if it satisfies

:{{EquationRef|6|(5){{spaces|2}}}}<math>\varphi(x)=\mu(|x|)</math> for some [[infinitely differentiable function]] <math>\mu:\R^+\to\R</math>,

then it is called a '''symmetric mollifier'''.

===Notes on Friedrichs' definition===
'''Note 1'''. When the theory of [[Distribution (mathematics)|distributions]] was still not widely known nor used,<ref>As when the paper {{Harv|Friedrichs|1944}} was published, few years before [[Laurent Schwartz]] widespread his work.</ref> property {{EquationNote|4|(3)}} above was formulated by saying that the [[convolution]] of the function ''<math>\scriptstyle\varphi_\epsilon</math>'' with a given function belonging to a proper [[Hilbert space|Hilbert]] or [[Banach space]] will [[Limit of a sequence#Metric spaces|converge]], in the metric of that space, as ''ε'' → 0  to that function:<ref>Obviously the [[topology]] with respect to convergence occurs is the one of the [[Hilbert space|Hilbert]] or [[Banach space]] considered.</ref> this is exactly what [[Kurt Otto Friedrichs|Friedrichs]] did.<ref>See {{harv|Friedrichs|1944|pp=136–138}}, properties '''PI''', '''PII''', '''PIII''' and their consequence '''PIII<sub>0</sub>'''.</ref> This also clarifies why mollifiers are related to [[approximate identity|approximate identities]].<ref name="Fredref">Also, in this respect, {{harvtxt|Friedrichs|1944|pp=132}} says:-"''The main tool for the proof is a certain class of smoothing operators approximating unity, the "mollifiers"''.</ref>

'''Note 2'''. As briefly pointed out in the "[[#Historical notes|Historical notes]]" section of this entry, originally, the term "mollifier" identified the following [[Convolution|convolution operator]]<ref name="Fredref"/><ref>See {{harv|Friedrichs|1944|p=137}}, [[paragraph]] 2, "''Integral operators''".</ref>:

:<math>\Phi_\epsilon(f)(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\varphi_\epsilon(x-y) f(y)\mathrm{d}y</math>

where <math>\varphi_\epsilon(x)=\epsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\epsilon)</math> and ''<math>\varphi</math>'' is a [[smooth function]] satisfying the first three conditions stated above and one or more supplementary conditions as positivity and symmetry.

== Concrete example ==
Consider the [[bump function]] ''<math>\varphi</math>''<math>(x)</math> of a [[Variable (mathematics)|variable]] in <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> defined by

:<math>\varphi(x) = \begin{cases} e^{-1/(1-|x|^2)}/I_n& \text{ if } |x| < 1\\
                 0& \text{ if } |x|\geq 1
                 \end{cases}</math>

where the numerical constant <math> I_n</math> ensures normalization. This function is [[Non-analytic smooth function|infinitely differentiable, non analytic]] with vanishing [[derivative]] for {{math|<nowiki>|</nowiki>''x''<nowiki>|</nowiki> {{=}} 1}}. ''<math>\varphi</math>'' can be therefore used as mollifier as described above: one can see that ''<math>\varphi</math>''<math>(x)</math> defines a ''positive and symmetric mollifier''.<ref>See {{Harv|Hörmander|1990|p=14}}, [[lemma (mathematics)|lemma]] 1.2.3.: the example is stated in implicit form by first defining 
:<math>f(t)=\exp({-1/t})</math> for <math>t\in\mathbb{R}_+</math>, 
and then considering 
:<math>f(x)=f\big(1-|x|^2\big)=\exp\big(-1/(1-|x|^2)\big)</math> for <math>x\in\mathbb{R}^n</math>.</ref>
[[File:Mollifier Illustration.svg|center|frame|The function ''<math>\varphi</math>''<math>(x)</math> in [[Dimension (mathematics)|dimension]] one]]

== Properties ==
All properties of a mollifier are related to its behaviour under the operation of [[convolution]]: we list the following ones, whose proofs can be found in every text on [[Distribution (mathematics)|distribution theory]].<ref>See for example {{Harv|Hörmander|1990}}.</ref>

=== Smoothing property===
For any distribution <math>T</math>, the following family of convolutions indexed by the [[real number]] <math>\epsilon</math>

:<math>T_\epsilon = T\ast\varphi_\epsilon</math>

where <math>\ast</math> denotes [[convolution]], is a family of [[smooth function]]s.

=== Approximation of identity===
For any distribution <math>T</math>, the following family of convolutions indexed by the [[real number]] <math>\epsilon</math> converges to <math>T</math>

:<math>\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}T_\epsilon = \lim_{\epsilon\to 0}T\ast\varphi_\epsilon=T\in D^\prime(\mathbb{R}^n)</math>

=== Support of convolution===
For any distribution <math>T</math>,

:<math>\operatorname{supp}T_\epsilon=\operatorname{supp}(T\ast\varphi_\epsilon)\subset\operatorname{supp}T+\operatorname{supp}\varphi_\epsilon</math>,

where <math>\operatorname{supp}</math> indicates the [[Distribution (mathematics)#Support of a distribution|support]] in the sense of distributions, and <math>+</math> indicates their [[Minkowski addition]].

== Applications ==
The basic application of mollifiers is to prove that properties valid for [[smooth function]]s are also valid in nonsmooth situations.

=== Product of distributions ===
In some theories of [[generalized function]]s, mollifiers are used to define the [[Generalized function#Multiplication of distributions|multiplication of distributions]]. Given two [[Distribution (mathematics)|distributions]] <math>S</math> and <math>T</math>, the limit of the product of the [[smooth function]] obtained from one operand via mollification, with the other operand defines, when it exists, their product in various theories of [[generalized function]]s:
 
:<math>S\cdot T := \lim_{\epsilon\to 0}S_\epsilon\cdot T=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}S\cdot T_\epsilon</math>.

=== "Weak=Strong" theorems ===
Mollifiers are used to prove the identity of two different kind of extension of differential operators: the strong extension and the [[Weak formulation|weak extension]]. The paper by Friedrichs which introduces mollifiers {{Harv|Friedrichs|1944}} illustrates this approach.

=== Smooth cutoff functions ===
By convolution of the [[indicator function|characteristic function]] of the [[unit ball]] <math>B_1 = \{x : |x|<1\}</math> with the [[smooth function]] ''<math>\varphi_{1/2}</math>'' (defined as in {{EquationNote|4|(3)}} with <math>\epsilon = 1/2</math>), one obtains the function

:<math>
\begin{align}
\chi_{B_1,1/2}(x)
&=\chi_{B_1}\ast\varphi_{1/2}(x)
\\
&=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\!\!\!\chi_{B_1}(x-y)\varphi_{1/2}(y)\mathrm{d}y
\\
&=\int_{B_{1/2}}\!\!\!
\chi_{B_1}(x-y) \varphi_{1/2}(y)\mathrm{d}y \ \ \ (\because\ \mathrm{supp}(\varphi_{1/2})=B_{1/2})
\end{align}
</math>

which is a [[smooth function]] equal to <math>1</math> on <math>B_{1/2} = \{ x: |x| < 1/2 \}</math>, with support contained in <math>B_{3/2}=\{ x: |x| < 3/2 \}</math>. This can be seen easily by observing that if <math>|x| \le 1/2</math> and <math>|y| \le 1/2</math> then <math> |x-y| \le 1</math>. Hence for <math>|x| \le 1/2</math>,
:<math>
\int_{B_{1/2}}\!\!\!\chi_{B_1}(x-y) \varphi_{1/2}(y)\mathrm{d}y= \int_{B_{1/2}}\!\!\!
 \varphi_{1/2}(y)\mathrm{d}y=1
</math>.
One can see how this construction can be generalized to obtain a smooth function identical to one on a [[neighbourhood (topology)|neighbourhood]] of a given [[compact set]], and equal to zero in every point whose [[distance]] from this set is greater than a given <math>\epsilon</math>.<ref>A proof of this fact can be found in {{Harv|Hörmander|1990|p=25}}, Theorem 1.4.1.</ref> Such a function is called a (smooth) '''cutoff function'''; these are used to eliminate singularities of a given ([[generalized function|generalized]]) [[function (mathematics)|function]] via [[multiplication]]. They leave unchanged the value of the multiplicand on a given [[set (mathematics)|set]], but modify its [[Distribution (mathematics)#Support of a distribution|support]]. Cutoff functions are used to construct [[Smooth function#Smooth partitions of unity|smooth partitions of unity]].
